strengths: The paper addresses a significant practical bottleneck: fine-grained MoEs can lose hardware efficiency despite favorable model FLOPs. Its analysis connects expert granularity and sparsity to activation storage, memory traffic, and tile-padding waste.

The core kernel contribution is substantial and well supported. Gather fusion in forward and backward passes, fused gradient epilogues, and asynchronous IO scheduling produce sizable improvements across multiple configurations. Comparisons include ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and an optimized DeepGEMM++ baseline.

Detailed runtime breakdowns and component experiments help explain the measured gains. The reported 45% activation-memory reduction and approximately 1.86× kernel throughput improvement are practically meaningful. The 64-H100 versus 96-H100 training experiment also provides evidence of benefits beyond isolated kernels.

Token rounding receives meaningful quality evaluation: multiple model configurations, up to 100B training tokens, eleven downstream tasks, several routing baselines, and ablations over rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes. Evaluation switches to token-choice routing, directly testing the proposed deployment procedure.
weaknesses: The token-rounding speedup does not establish an end-to-end training benefit. Section 6.3.3 explicitly excludes the router, although Algorithm 4 adds per-expert sorting and assignment processing. This overhead could offset the reported approximately 16% kernel improvement, especially as the number of experts grows. Claims of additional training-throughput improvement require measurements including routing, metadata construction, and the full training step.

Several rounding guarantees are overstated. Default deterministic nearest rounding does not generally preserve total assignments in expectation without assumptions on token-count distributions. Actual assignment counts and training FLOPs should be reported. Algorithm 6 also incorrectly claims a per-expert deviation bounded by half a tile: with tile size 128 and frequencies (179, 179, 154), its sequential rule produces (128, 256, 128), giving a deviation of 77 for the second expert.

The distributed evidence is limited to one FSDP configuration and compares different GPU counts, without a same-hardware throughput or scaling study. Expert parallelism is left to future work, although it changes gather and communication costs central to the proposed advantage. Experiments use H100s; the Blackwell implementation discussion is not accompanied by corresponding performance evidence.

The claim of preserving quality needs qualification. Results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, and Tables 7–8 show degradation when average expert occupancy approaches one tile. Because token rounding makes assignments depend on other tokens in the microbatch, its training-time future-token dependence also warrants explicit analysis. Switching to token-choice evaluation is useful evidence but does not establish general robustness across scales and occupancy distributions.

Numerical correctness is insufficiently documented for a custom training-kernel paper. There are no systematic forward and gradient error comparisons against a reference. The top-K implementation overwrites low FP32 mantissa bits, potentially changing selections for close scores, but routing disagreement rates and their training impact are not measured.

The novelty is primarily in the integrated systems design. The paper acknowledges prior use of the gradient reformulation in Megatron and of ping-pong scheduling elsewhere. The 'minimum possible' activation-memory claim is also stronger than the analysis establishes: it concerns retained activations under particular recomputation assumptions, while transient buffers and routing metadata remain. These distinctions should be clearer.

strengths: The core systems contribution is meaningful: SonicMoE combines memory-efficient backward computation, fused gathers, epilogue fusion, and asynchronous scheduling to address the increasing IO cost of fine-grained MoEs. Appendix C provides a sound derivation of the main gradient reformulation.

The kernel evaluation is extensive and includes relevant baselines: ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and DeepGEMM. Constructing an optimized DeepGEMM++ baseline strengthens the comparisons. Figure 6 reports substantial forward and backward improvements, while Figure 13 reports a 45% activation-memory reduction for the fine-grained 7B configuration.

Detailed profiling and component experiments substantiate the engineering decisions. In particular, the gather-fusion comparisons and controlled scatter-versus-gather aggregation experiment help explain the performance gains rather than merely reporting aggregate speedups.

Token rounding receives substantial empirical quality evaluation: five pretraining configurations, 11 downstream tasks, several routing baselines, and ablations over rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes. Table 3 provides encouraging evidence that switching to token-choice routing at evaluation preserves quality in the tested settings.
weaknesses: The claimed additional training speedup from token rounding is not established end to end. Section 6.3.3 explicitly excludes router runtime, although Algorithm 4 introduces expert-wise sorting and additional routing operations. The reported approximately 16% improvement therefore measures expert computation, not the complete training benefit. Router-inclusive latency and time-to-quality comparisons are necessary.

The rounding guarantees contain substantive errors. Default nearest rounding does not generally preserve the total assignment count in expectation without assumptions on the count distribution. Moreover, Equation 14's simultaneous per-expert and aggregate error bounds are impossible in general: with tile size 128 and counts (170, 170, 172), satisfying the per-expert bound of 64 forces all counts to 128, creating aggregate error 128. Algorithm 6 can bound aggregate error by choosing a farther rounding direction, but then violates the stated per-expert bound.

Distributed applicability is insufficiently demonstrated. The end-to-end experiment compares 64 H100s against 96 H100s, without a matched-hardware comparison or scaling curve. Its reported rates imply approximately 42% greater throughput per GPU, rather than directly demonstrating the claimed 50% same-hardware training improvement. Expert parallelism is left to future work, despite its importance for the large sparse models motivating the paper; all reported performance plots also concern H100 rather than validating the Blackwell discussion.

The quality-preservation claim needs qualification. The routing experiments cover 0.5B–1.8B models without reported seed variation or uncertainty, and several differences are small. Tables 7–8 show perplexity degradation when average expert occupancy approaches one tile. Because routing decisions depend on other tokens in the microbatch, the extent of future-token dependence and train–test mismatch also deserves direct analysis.

Several ingredients are established techniques: Appendix C acknowledges the equivalent gradient computation in Megatron, while ping-pong scheduling and gather fusion have prior implementations. The strongest novelty is their effective integration and specialization. Claims of the 'minimum possible' activation footprint additionally lack a formal lower bound and should distinguish retained activations from transient buffers and routing metadata.

Numerical correctness and reproducibility need stronger documentation. Section 4.3 overwrites low FP32 mantissa bits during top-K selection, which can change assignments for closely spaced scores, but reports no mismatch rates or training sensitivity. Explicit forward/gradient error tests, benchmark timing procedures, and complete distributed-run configurations would make the systems results easier to verify.

strengths: SonicMoE addresses a significant practical bottleneck in fine-grained MoE training. Its combination of activation-memory reduction, gather and epilogue fusion, and asynchronous scheduling forms a substantial systems contribution.

The core backward reformulation is well motivated and algebraically sound: computing router-score gradients through intermediate activations avoids retaining large expert outputs without additional GEMMs. Reported activation-memory savings reach 45% against ScatterMoE.

Kernel evaluation is unusually extensive, covering multiple model configurations, forward and backward execution, and relevant baselines including ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and an optimized DeepGEMM implementation. Detailed profiling and component ablations provide convincing explanations for the performance gains.

Token rounding receives meaningful quality evaluation across five training configurations, 11 downstream tasks, and ablations of rounding rules, microbatch sizes, and tile sizes. Evaluating with ordinary token-choice routing appropriately tests the training–inference mismatch.
weaknesses: The additional end-to-end speedup attributed to token rounding is not established. Section 6.3.3 explicitly excludes router runtime, although Algorithm 4 adds expert-wise sorting and routing-metadata processing. The reported approximately 16% improvement concerns expert computation; complete routing-inclusive step timings and time-to-quality comparisons are needed.

Distributed evidence is limited to one 7B configuration and compares different GPU counts: 213 billion tokens/day on 64 H100s versus 225 billion on 96. This is encouraging but does not isolate the claimed 50% throughput improvement under matched conditions. Expert-parallel communication is untested, and the reported performance experiments do not validate the Blackwell implementation.

Some rounding guarantees are incorrect or insufficiently qualified. Deterministic nearest rounding does not generally preserve total assignments in expectation without distributional assumptions. Algorithm 6 also cannot guarantee its stated per-expert error bound of half a tile: with tile size 128 and counts beginning 179, 179, it rounds the first to 128 and the second to 256, producing an error of 77. These claims should be corrected, and actual assignment/FLOP budgets reported.

The quality-preservation claim needs qualification. Results lack repeated seeds or uncertainty estimates, and quality experiments stop at 1.8B parameters. Tables 7–8 already show degradation when average expert occupancy reaches one tile, precisely where padding savings become attractive. The evidence supports approximate preservation within the tested occupancy regime, not an unrestricted no-loss claim.

Novelty and memory-optimality claims are stronger than demonstrated. The paper acknowledges that Megatron already uses the same efficient score-gradient computation, so novelty primarily lies in kernel integration and scheduling. The claimed minimum activation footprint is not backed by a lower-bound argument, and cached activations should be distinguished more clearly from peak memory, which includes temporary expert outputs and routing metadata.

strengths: A practically significant systems contribution addressing activation memory and IO bottlenecks in fine-grained MoE training. The backward reformulation is mathematically justified and avoids caching expert outputs without additional GEMMs.

Convincing kernel-level evaluation across H100 and B300 GPUs, multiple model configurations, and several relevant baselines. DeepGEMM++ incorporates optimized surrounding operations and the same backward computation path, making it a useful strong comparison.

Substantial measured improvements, including 45% lower activation memory versus ScatterMoE for the fine-grained 7B configuration. Distributed training results provide additional evidence of practical utility.

Detailed implementation explanations, component profiling, and ablations support the engineering contribution. Token rounding is also evaluated through actual language-model pretraining, downstream tasks, and sensitivity studies.
weaknesses: The claimed additional 16% training speedup from token rounding is not established end to end: Section 6.3.3 explicitly excludes router time, although Algorithm 4 adds expert-wise sorting. Full training-step measurements including routing overhead are necessary.

The claim that token rounding preserves assignment counts in expectation does not generally hold for the default deterministic nearest-rounding rule. It holds for the described stochastic alternative. Actual assignment counts and training FLOPs should be reported to substantiate compute-matched comparisons.

Quality preservation is demonstrated only at 0.5B–1.8B scale, without reported training-seed variability. Tables 7–8 show degradation when average expert occupancy reaches one tile, limiting the broad claims about highly sparse regimes. Batch-dependent routing also introduces a train–inference mismatch whose larger-scale consequences remain untested.

Distributed evidence is limited to one FSDP configuration comparing different GPU counts. Matched-hardware comparisons and expert-parallel experiments are needed to establish how much of the kernel advantage survives communication and smaller local expert batches.

Novelty is primarily in integration and implementation: asynchronous scheduling is established, and the memory-efficient gradient path also appears in Megatron. Reproducibility would benefit from explicit timing protocols and numerical-gradient accuracy results; Section 4.1.2 also gives a score-gradient expression inconsistent with the correct Algorithm 3 and Appendix C.

strengths: The core systems contribution is practically meaningful: SonicMoE combines backward-pass memory savings, gather and epilogue fusion, and asynchronous IO scheduling to address the increasing overhead of fine-grained MoEs.

The performance evaluation covers both H100 and B300 GPUs, multiple expert configurations, and substantial baselines. DeepGEMM++ incorporates optimized surrounding kernels and the same backward computational path, making it a particularly useful comparison. Reported gains extend beyond comparisons with older implementations.

The main backward derivation in Appendix C is sound: computing routing-score gradients through the intermediate activation avoids retaining expert outputs. The reported 45% activation-memory reduction and substantial forward/backward speedups provide concrete evidence of value.

Detailed kernel breakdowns, component benchmarks, baseline source references, and training configurations support the empirical contribution. Token rounding is also evaluated through actual pretraining, 11 downstream tasks, and ablations of rounding strategy, microbatch size, and tile size.
weaknesses: The additional training-speed claim for token rounding is not established end to end. Section 6.3.3 explicitly excludes routing runtime, although Algorithm 4 adds expert-wise sorting and assignment processing. The reported 15.9% improvement therefore concerns the expert-computation kernels; routing-inclusive step times are necessary to substantiate the broader training-throughput claim.

The distributed evaluation is limited to one comparison using different GPU counts: 64 H100s for SonicMoE versus 96 for ScatterMoE. This supports improved resource efficiency but does not isolate a same-hardware speedup. There is no corresponding full-training comparison against DeepGEMM++, and expert-parallel communication is left to future work.

Some mathematical claims require correction. Default deterministic nearest rounding does not generally preserve assignment counts in expectation without distributional assumptions. Algorithm 6 also does not satisfy its claimed per-expert half-tile error bound: with tile size 128 and counts (180, 180), it rounds to (128, 256), yielding an error of 76 for the second expert. These issues affect auxiliary routing guarantees rather than the core kernel derivation.

The evidence supports similar routing quality in the tested settings, but not an unrestricted 'without quality loss' claim. Quality experiments reach 1.8B parameters, report no seed variability or confidence intervals, and show degradation when average expert occupancy approaches one tile. Batch-dependent routing also introduces a training/inference mismatch; switching to token choice at evaluation is a useful test, but does not establish robustness at larger scales.

Novelty is primarily in systems integration and implementation. Ping-Pong scheduling and several fusion techniques are established, and the paper acknowledges that Megatron already uses the memory-efficient gradient computation. The contribution would be positioned more precisely by distinguishing these inherited ingredients from the new scheduling and fusion combinations.

Several claims and reporting details need tighter qualification. The minimum-memory argument concerns cached activations under specific recomputation assumptions, while temporary expert outputs and routing metadata remain. Section 4.1.2 also states a routing-gradient identity inconsistent with the correct Algorithm 3 and Appendix C. Benchmark timing methodology and numerical-equivalence testing are insufficiently documented for fully independent verification.

strengths: A substantial systems contribution addressing an important bottleneck in fine-grained MoE training. The combination of backward gather fusion, activation-memory reduction, and asynchronous compute/IO overlap is technically well motivated.

Broad kernel evaluation across H100 and B300 GPUs, multiple expert granularities, and contemporary MoE configurations shows consistent improvements. The optimized DeepGEMM++ baseline is a particularly valuable comparison.

Detailed runtime breakdowns and component experiments substantiate the implementation choices. The reported 45% activation-memory reduction and distributed 7B training throughput provide concrete evidence of practical value.

Token rounding is a useful hardware-aware routing idea. Training experiments across five configurations and eleven downstream tasks, together with rounding, microbatch, and tile-size ablations, provide encouraging evidence that switching to token-choice routing at evaluation can preserve quality.
weaknesses: The additional end-to-end speedup claimed for token rounding is not established: Section 6.3.3 explicitly excludes router runtime. Algorithm 4 introduces per-expert sorting across tokens, whose overhead could offset the saved GEMM time. Full routing-inclusive step latency and training throughput are needed.

Some rounding guarantees are incorrect or insufficiently qualified. Deterministic nearest rounding does not generally preserve total assignments in expectation without assumptions about token-count residues. Algorithm 6 also fails its claimed per-expert error bound of half a tile: with tile size 128 and counts (50, 50, 28), it returns (0, 128, 0), giving an error of 78 for the second expert.

Distributed evidence is limited to one 7B configuration and compares 64 GPUs against 96 GPUs. This supports practical promise but does not isolate a same-resource speedup or establish scaling behavior. Expert-parallel communication, especially relevant to the largest model configurations, remains untested.

The quality-preservation claim needs qualification. No repeated-seed uncertainty is reported, quality experiments stop at 1.8B parameters, and Tables 7–8 show degradation when average tokens per expert approach one tile. Large-model kernel benchmarks do not establish quality preservation at those scales.

Novelty is strongest in the integrated kernel design rather than every individual component: Ping-Pong scheduling is established, and Appendix C acknowledges the same router-gradient formulation in Megatron. The claimed minimum activation memory also needs a precise scope distinguishing cached activations from transient buffers and routing metadata.
